title: Hydrogen Cars Are Not Dead… Yet

body_markdown:
It’s the fuel of the future. Or so we’ve been led to believe for decades. Yet hydrogen has, so far, failed to make a significant impact on the auto industry.


This is not for want of trying, with major manufacturers investing heavily in H2 development, but very, very few of us are actually driving hydrogen cars.


The attraction is obvious. Hydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe. Combine it with oxygen, either through combustion or in a fuel cell, and the only emission is water.


It sounds like the perfect environmentally-friendly transport solution, but hydrogen brings a raft of problems. First, it has to be produced at scale. In an ideal scenario, it would be extracted from water via electrolysis, but that uses a lot of electricity. It can also be gathered from hydrocarbon fuels, although that rather defeats the whole green idea.


Next up, you’ve got the issue of storage. Unlike fossil fuels, hydrogen’s natural state is a gas, so to store it in a space-efficient manner, it needs to be kept under extreme pressure or extremely low temperature. The diminutive size of hydrogen molecules also means that it has a tendency to escape, so creating leak-free storage systems, both at filling stations and in vehicles, is a big challenge.


Then you’ve got energy density. By *weight* , hydrogen packs roughly three times as much energy as gasoline, which sounds great until you remember that storage problem. Compared to the same *volume* of gasoline, the numbers get flipped, and liquid hydrogen becomes the loser, by a similar margin.


Finally, there’s getting that hydrogen into filling stations and thus into vehicles. According to the Department of Energy’s Alternative Fuels Data Center, there were just 54 hydrogen stations across the U.S. in 2024, with a further 20 planned. Almost all are in California. Meanwhile, if you need to fill up your gasoline car, it’s estimated that there are more than 150,000 places to pump.


Turning hydrogen into momentum can be achieved by exploding it in an engine, or converting it to electricity in a fuel cell, and carmakers have tried both.


In the 2000s, BMW and Mazda tried out H2 combustion in the 7-Series and RX-8. For BMW, a V-12 was the chosen solution, while Mazda ran a rotary in the RX-8. On the plus side, these cars might still appeal to enthusiasts, but trunk space was taken up with hydrogen storage, and their performance was down on their gasoline equivalents. A dead end, then.


Mazda


As if the RX-8 wasn’t weird enough with its “freestyle” doors and Renesis rotary engine that needed careful tending, Mazda decided to fuel it with hydrogen. Or at least it did for a pilot program on Norway’s so-called Hydrogen Highway. Technically, it was a dual-fuel car, retaining a small petrol tank for emergencies, but when a colleague drove one, much of the hydrogen evaporated overnight, and he was forced to stop every 50 miles to fill up with regular gas to complete the journey. The car was never made available to the public.


Honda


Fuel cells showed more promise, dating back to the 1990s with Honda’s FCX models, including the Clarity, which actually went on sale to the public in 2007. The numbers are not exactly earth-shattering. 200 Hondas were available to lease worldwide, of which 48 reached the U.S.


The Toyota Mirai has fared better. Over two generations, around 25,000 have been built, with more than 11,000 sold in America in a dozen years. That’s less than half the number of Camrys that find buyers *in a month* . On a more positive note, the Mirai can potentially take you up to 400 miles on a full tank of H2.


Toyota


In 2018, the Mercedes-Benz GLC F-Cell was the first car in the world to combine a fuel cell with a lithium-ion battery pack that could also be charged via a plug. A pair of carbon fiber tanks held 9.7 lbs of hydrogen at 700 bar (over 10,000 psi). There was a reasonable 200 hp and a range of almost 300 miles. A few examples were available to lease in Germany and Japan before Mercedes axed it and abandoned fuel cells in favor of BEVs.


Mercedes-Benz


According to a report by[The Korean Car Blog](https://thekoreancarblog.com/leaked-kia-document-next-gen-carnival-hydrogen-carnival-new-sorento-ev7/) , a hydrogen fuel cell will be offered in the next Kia Carnival from 2029. Most likely, it will use the same powertrain as the recently-launched Hyundai NEXO SUV, available to Californians, which claims a range of 447 miles and five-minute fill-ups.


Honda lists the CR-V Fuel Cell as a Future Vehicle on its website, with its bid for your bucks resting on the ability to refuel with hydrogen and/or recharge at home or an EV charging station. High-pressure tanks behind the rear seats hold 9.5 lbs of compressed hydrogen, and there’s a 17.7 kWh battery pack. Together, they’ll deliver a potential range of 270 miles for California drivers who aren’t quite ready to go all-in on H2.


BMW


BMW also hasn’t thrown in the towel. In fact, the fuel cell-powered iX5 Hydrogen is getting very close to production. As you can imagine, it runs the same electric powertrain as the iX5, but packs a smaller battery pack that gets continuously charged by a fuel cell. The gas is stored in BMW’s new Hydrogen Flat Storage system, which features seven hydrogen tanks under the car’s floor, holding the H2 at a pressure of 700 bar (over 10,000 psi). BMW claims it will have a range of 385 miles and be as quick and easy to refuel as a gasoline car. That would be impressive if it wasn’t for the fact that the battery-electric iX5 has an EPA range of 450 miles. The EV-only version will take longer to recharge, though, going from 10 to 80 percent in 22 minutes on a high-speed charger.


It’s hard to imagine that really being a sticking point, except perhaps for very high-mileage business users. With the number of EV charging stations rapidly ramping up (80,000 public chargers at the last count) and charging speeds increasing, hydrogen may not have a future at all. That hasn’t stopped manufacturers from experimenting, though.
